questions.question: Name the four components of blood and give the function of each; then list the four functions of blood as a whole.
questions.expected_answer: Plasma: liquid that transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, salts, hormones, urea and carbon dioxide. Red blood cells: contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen. White blood cells: defend against infection by engulfing microbes and making antibodies. Platelets: cause clotting at wounds. Functions of blood: transport, defence against disease, clotting, and regulation of body temperature by carrying heat.

questions.question: Trace the path of blood through the double circulation starting at the vena cava, naming each chamber and vessel and stating whether the blood is oxygenated or deoxygenated.
questions.expected_answer: Vena cava (deoxygenated) → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery (deoxygenated) → lungs, where carbon dioxide is lost and oxygen gained → pulmonary vein (oxygenated) → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta (oxygenated) → body, where oxygen is delivered → vena cava. Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit; the left ventricle is thicker because it pumps to the whole body.

questions.question: Compare arteries, veins and capillaries in terms of wall thickness, pressure, valves and function, and explain why defining arteries by oxygen content is a mistake.
questions.expected_answer: Arteries: thick, muscular, elastic walls; high pressure; no valves; carry blood away from the heart. Veins: thinner walls, wider lumen; low pressure; valves prevent backflow; carry blood towards the heart. Capillaries: walls one cell thick; low pressure; site of exchange of oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide and wastes with cells. Arteries must be defined by direction because the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood to the heart.
